sessions.title: Jesus Wept
sessions.intro: Lazarus of Bethany had died, and by the time Jesus arrived he had lain in the grave four days. John records that Jesus loved Lazarus and his sisters, Martha and Mary. When Mary heard that the Master had come and was calling for her, she rose quickly and went to Him.
notice: Mary falls at His feet and says what Martha had also said: “Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” Jesus doesn’t argue with her or explain.
When He saw her weeping, and those with her weeping too, “he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled.”
He asks to be taken to the place of their grief: “Where have ye laid him?”
“Jesus wept.” He had already told Martha that her brother would rise again (John 11:23), and soon He would call Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43). John records His tears all the same.
Those watching read His tears as love: “Behold how he loved him!”
ponder: What does it mean to you that the Savior wept, even after saying that Lazarus would rise again?
Mary brought Him her grief just as it was. Is there something you would like to bring to Him just as it is?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about any sorrow you carry, or about someone who is grieving, and ask for the comfort His Son gives.

verses.text: Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see.
Jesus wept.
Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!

sessions.title: He Stayed a Little Longer
sessions.intro: The risen Savior had been teaching the people gathered at the temple in the land Bountiful. Then He told them His time was at hand: they should go home, ponder what He had said, and prepare their minds for the next day, for He was going to the Father (3 Nephi 17:1–4).
notice: Before leaving, He looked at them again. They were in tears, looking at Him “as if they would ask him to tarry a little longer with them.” He answered what they hadn’t said aloud.
He described His compassion as filling Him: “Behold, my bowels are filled with compassion towards you.”
He named many kinds of affliction, down to anyone “afflicted in any manner,” and said, “Bring them hither and I will heal them.”
He saw their faith, not only their need: “I see that your faith is sufficient that I should heal you.”
“He did heal them every one as they were brought forth unto him.” Then they bowed at His feet, and many kissed His feet and bathed them with their tears.
ponder: He noticed what the people longed for before they asked. What would you hope He notices in you?
What might it have meant to the people that He healed them “every one”?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about anyone who needs healing, yourself included, and ask that His Son’s compassion reach them.

verses.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had thus spoken, he cast his eyes round about again on the multitude, and beheld they were in tears, and did look steadfastly upon him as if they would ask him to tarry a little longer with them.
And he said unto them: Behold, my bowels are filled with compassion towards you.

Have ye any that are sick among you? Bring them hither. Have ye any that are lame, or blind, or halt, or maimed, or leprous, or that are withered, or that are deaf, or that are afflicted in any manner? Bring them hither and I will heal them, for I have compassion upon you; my bowels are filled with mercy.
For I perceive that ye desire that I should show unto you what I have done unto your brethren at Jerusalem, for I see that your faith is sufficient that I should heal you.

And it came to pass that when he had thus spoken, all the multitude, with one accord, did go forth with their sick and their afflicted, and their lame, and with their blind, and with their dumb, and with all them that were afflicted in any manner; and he did heal them every one as they were brought forth unto him.

And they did all, both they who had been healed and they who were whole, bow down at his feet, and did worship him; and as many as could come for the multitude did kiss his feet, insomuch that they did bathe his feet with their tears.

sessions.title: Lord, Save Me
sessions.intro: Jesus sent His disciples ahead by ship while He sent the multitudes away, and then went up a mountain alone to pray. Out in the middle of the sea, the ship was tossed with waves, for the wind was contrary (Matthew 14:22–24).
notice: He came to them “in the fourth watch of the night,” walking on the water toward the tossing ship.
When they cried out in fear, He answered “straightway”: “Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.”
Peter asked to come to Him, and Jesus answered with one word: “Come.”
Peter began to sink when “he saw the wind boisterous.” His prayer was three words: “Lord, save me.”
“Immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him.” Only then did He ask, “wherefore didst thou doubt?”
ponder: Peter began to sink when he saw the wind and was afraid. What helps you keep coming toward the Savior when you are afraid?
Peter’s prayer was short and honest. What short prayer might you offer today?
What might it mean for you that the Savior reached out “immediately”?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, tell Heavenly Father about whatever feels like wind and waves right now, and ask for help to keep coming toward His Son.

verses.text: And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
And when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear.
But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.
And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?

sessions.title: Not My Will, but Thine
sessions.intro: After the Passover meal with His Apostles, Jesus went out, as He often did, to the Mount of Olives, and His disciples followed Him. Matthew names the place where He prayed: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36).
notice: Before praying for Himself, He spoke to His disciples: “Pray that ye enter not into temptation.”
He went “about a stone’s cast” from them, knelt down, and prayed.
He told His Father honestly what He wished, “remove this cup from me,” and then yielded His will: “nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
Heaven sent help: “there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him.”
As His agony deepened, so did His prayer: “being in an agony he prayed more earnestly.”

insights.text: In a revelation to Joseph Smith, the Savior described His suffering for all in His own words: it caused Him “to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit.” He adds, “I partook and finished my preparations unto the children of men.” The revelation doesn’t name a place; many readers connect it with Luke’s account, where “his sweat was as it were great drops of blood.”

ponder: What do you notice about how honestly the Savior spoke with His Father?
An angel came to strengthen Him. What might that suggest about how Heavenly Father helps in hard moments?
What would it mean for you to pray, “not my will, but thine, be done”?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, thank Heavenly Father for what His Son suffered, and talk with Him honestly about anything you are finding hard to accept.

verses.text: ¶ And he came out, and went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed him.
And when he was at the place, he said unto them, Pray that ye enter not into temptation.
And he was withdrawn from them about a stone’s cast, and kneeled down, and prayed,
Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.
And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him.
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent;
But if they would not repent they must suffer even as I;

Which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit—and would that I might not drink the bitter cup, and shrink—
Nevertheless, glory be to the Father, and I partook and finished my preparations unto the children of men.

sessions.title: Lovest Thou Me?
sessions.intro: After His Resurrection, Jesus showed Himself to several disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. They had fished all night and caught nothing; at His word their net filled, and on the shore He gave them bread and fish. Not long before, Peter had three times denied being His disciple (John 18:17, 25–27).
notice: Jesus calls him by name each time: “Simon, son of Jonas.”
He asks the same question three times, and the third time “Peter was grieved.”
Peter doesn’t promise to do better. He rests on what Jesus knows: “Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee.”
Each answer is met with a charge, not a rebuke: “Feed my lambs.” “Feed my sheep.”
Soon after, Jesus said to him, Follow me (John 21:19).
ponder: Peter had denied three times that he was His disciple; here Jesus asks three times. Might the two be connected? John doesn’t say. What do you notice about how He treated Peter?
If the Savior asked you, “Lovest thou me?” what would you want to say?
Who might be the ‘lambs’ and ‘sheep’ around you?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about your love for His Son, and ask whom you might care for in His name.

verses.text: ¶ So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.
He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

sessions.title: This Man Receiveth Sinners
sessions.intro: Publicans and sinners were drawing near to hear Jesus, and some Pharisees and scribes complained. Jesus answered with three stories of something lost and found: a sheep, a coin, and a son (Luke 15). This is the first.
sessions.question: Why did Jesus welcome sinners and eat with them?

insights.text: The people drawing close were “publicans and sinners.” The Guide to the Scriptures explains that publicans were tax collectors who “were generally hated by the Jews.” Jesus didn’t keep His distance from the people others avoided. His critics noticed that He “receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.”

In His answer, the shepherd doesn’t wait for the lost sheep to come back. He goes “after that which is lost, until he find it,” and then “layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” There is no scolding in the story, only searching and joy.
Jesus applies the story Himself: “joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.” The joy He describes is over a sinner who repents.

When His disciples were asked a similar question at a feast in Levi’s house (Luke 5:29), Jesus answered, “They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

ponder: Who might feel like the one sheep that wandered? How does the Savior see them?
What does it suggest about the Savior that heaven rejoices over one person who repents?
Is there someone you could welcome the way He did?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about anyone who feels far away, perhaps yourself, and thank Him that His Son goes after the one.

verses.text: Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him.
And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.
¶ And he spake this parable unto them, saying,
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
But their scribes and Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?
And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.
I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

sources.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Publican
sources.excerpt: In ancient Rome, a collector of taxes for the government. Publicans were generally hated by the Jews.

sessions.title: Rest unto Your Souls
sessions.intro: Just before these words, Jesus thanked His Father for revealing truth to ‘babes’ rather than to the wise and prudent, and taught that the Son reveals the Father (Matthew 11:25–27). Then He turned to everyone who is weary.
sessions.question: What kind of rest does the Savior offer?

insights.text: The invitation is to “all ye that labour and are heavy laden.” Being weary or burdened is not a reason to stay away from Him. It is the very condition He names in His invitation.

The rest He offers doesn’t come from having no yoke at all. He says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me.” The Guide to the Scriptures explains that a yoke harnesses animals or people together, and that “the yoke of Christ is a symbol for discipleship.”
When He invites us to learn of Him, the one thing He tells us about Himself is that He is “meek and lowly in heart.” The promise follows: “ye shall find rest unto your souls.”

The Guide to the Scriptures describes rest as “the enjoyment of peace and freedom from worry and turmoil,” promised to the Lord’s faithful followers “during this life,” with a place of rest prepared for them in the next.

ponder: What are you carrying right now that you would like to bring to Him?
How might being yoked with the Savior make a burden lighter, even when the burden doesn’t disappear?
What could you learn from Him about being ‘meek and lowly in heart’?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, tell Heavenly Father what feels heavy right now, and ask for the rest His Son promised.

verses.text: ¶ Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

sources.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Yoke
sources.excerpt: A device put around the necks of animals or men to harness them together. The yoke of Christ is a symbol for discipleship, whereas the yoke of bondage is a symbol for oppression.

sources.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Rest
sources.excerpt: The enjoyment of peace and freedom from worry and turmoil. The Lord has promised such rest to His faithful followers during this life. He has also prepared a place of rest for them in the next life.

sessions.title: Jesus Stood Still
sessions.intro: Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, where He had told His disciples He would be betrayed and crucified (Matthew 20:17–19). As He left Jericho, a great multitude followed Him, and two blind men by the wayside heard that He was passing by.
sessions.question: Why did Jesus ask, “What will ye that I shall do unto you?”

insights.text: The crowd told the two men to hold their peace, but they cried out all the more. With a great multitude around Him, Jesus “stood still, and called them.”
Matthew doesn’t say why Jesus asked. What the account shows is that He let them say, in their own words, what they wanted, “Lord, that our eyes may be opened,” and then He gave them exactly that.

Earlier in the same chapter He asked a similar question, “What wilt thou?”, of the mother of Zebedee’s children, James and John (Matthew 4:21). She asked that her sons sit on His right hand and His left in His kingdom, and He answered, “Ye know not what ye ask.” Matthew doesn’t compare the two scenes, but the same kind of question drew a very different request.
Matthew names what moved Him: “Jesus had compassion on them, and touched their eyes.” Once they could see, “they followed him.”

ponder: If the Savior stood still and asked you this question today, what would you ask for?
Why might it matter to put our desires into words when we pray?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, tell Heavenly Father plainly what you desire, as these two men did, and ask for help to want what His Son wants for you.

verses.text: ¶ And, behold, two blind men sitting by the way side, when they heard that Jesus passed by, cried out, saying, Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David.
And the multitude rebuked them, because they should hold their peace: but they cried the more, saying, Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David.
And Jesus stood still, and called them, and said, What will ye that I shall do unto you?
They say unto him, Lord, that our eyes may be opened.
So Jesus had compassion on them, and touched their eyes: and immediately their eyes received sight, and they followed him.
¶ Then came to him the mother of Zebedee’s children with her sons, worshipping him, and desiring a certain thing of him.
And he said unto her, What wilt thou? She saith unto him, Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom.

But Jesus answered and said, Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? They say unto him, We are able.

sessions.title: The Vine and the Branches
sessions.intro: On the night before His Crucifixion, Jesus taught His disciples that He is the true vine and that His Father is the husbandman who tends it (John 15:1–2). Then He spoke of what the branches need.
sessions.question: What does it mean to abide in Christ?

insights.text: Abiding goes both ways: “Abide in me, and I in you.” The Savior speaks of it not only as our staying with Him, but as His remaining in us.
In the image, fruit depends on the branch staying joined to the vine: a branch “cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine.” Then He says it plainly: “without me ye can do nothing.”
A few verses later He describes abiding in terms of love: “continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love.” He adds that He abides in His Father’s love the same way.
He tells them why He taught this: “that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.”

ponder: What helps you stay connected to the Savior from day to day?
What might it mean that He also abides in you?
What kind of ‘fruit’ would you like your life to bear?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, ask Heavenly Father to help you stay close to His Son, and talk with Him about what makes that hard or easy right now.

verses.text: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love.
If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.

sessions.title: A High Priest Who Understands
sessions.intro: The Epistle to the Hebrews calls Jesus “a great high priest.” Earlier it explains that He was made “like unto his brethren,” “that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest” (Hebrews 2:17). These verses explain what that means for us.
sessions.question: Does the Savior understand what I’m going through?

insights.text: Hebrews says it with a double negative: we have not a high priest “which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.” In other words, He can be.
He “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.” Hebrews explains why that matters: “in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.”
Because He understands, the invitation is to come closer, not to hide: “come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.”

ponder: What would it mean to come to Him ‘boldly’ with what you are facing?
How might knowing that He understands change the way you pray?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about something you’ve felt no one could understand, and ask for grace to help in your time of need.

verses.text: Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.

sessions.title: My Peace I Give unto You
sessions.intro: On the night before His Crucifixion, Jesus told His disciples that He would soon leave them. He promised that the Father would send the Comforter, the Holy Ghost, to teach them and bring His words to their remembrance (John 14:26). Then He said this.
ponder: He says His peace is given “not as the world giveth.” How might His peace be different?
He spoke these words on the night before His own suffering. What does that suggest about the peace He offers?
Is there a troubled or afraid place in your heart you would like to bring to Him?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, tell Heavenly Father what is troubling your heart, and ask for the peace His Son promised.

verses.text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.

sessions.title: He Hath Borne Our Griefs
sessions.intro: Centuries before the Savior’s birth, Isaiah wrote of one who would bear the griefs and sorrows of others. The Book of Mormon prophet Abinadi quoted these words and taught that they speak of Christ (Mosiah 14–15), and Matthew saw them fulfilled when Jesus healed the sick (Matthew 8:16–17).
ponder: Notice how often Isaiah says ‘our’ and ‘we.’ What do these words suggest about whom He suffered for?
What griefs or sorrows would you like to let Him carry?
What might it mean that “with his stripes we are healed”?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, thank Heavenly Father for His Son, who carried griefs and sorrows that were not His own.

verses.text: ¶ Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

sessions.title: Look unto Me in Every Thought
sessions.intro: In April 1829, at Harmony, Pennsylvania, the Lord gave this revelation to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, soon after Oliver began serving as scribe for the translation of the Book of Mormon. In it the Lord names Himself: Jesus Christ, the Son of God (verse 21).
ponder: He says, “I do not condemn you,” and then, “go your ways and sin no more.” How do His mercy and His direction fit together?
What might it look like to turn one ordinary thought toward Him today?
Why might He invite us to behold His wounds?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, tell Heavenly Father about a doubt or fear you carry, and ask for help to look to His Son in your thoughts.

verses.text: Therefore, fear not, little flock; do good; let earth and hell combine against you, for if ye are built upon my rock, they cannot prevail.
Behold, I do not condemn you; go your ways and sin no more; perform with soberness the work which I have commanded you.
Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.
Behold the wounds which pierced my side, and also the prints of the nails in my hands and feet; be faithful, keep my commandments, and ye shall inherit the kingdom of heaven. Amen.

sessions.title: Come unto Christ
sessions.intro: Moroni wrote these words as he finished the Book of Mormon. His father had been killed and his people destroyed, and he remained alone to complete the record (Mormon 8:3). Near the very end, he invites us.
ponder: Moroni says we may be perfect “in Christ” and “by his grace.” What does that suggest about who makes us whole?
What is one way you could come unto Christ today?
Where would it help you to remember that His grace is “sufficient for you”?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, talk with Heavenly Father about coming closer to His Son, and ask for His grace in what you cannot do alone.

verses.text: Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.

sessions.title: We Talk of Christ
sessions.intro: Nephi wrote to persuade his children and his people to believe in Christ. Though they still kept the law of Moses, they looked forward with steadfastness to Christ (2 Nephi 25:23–24). In this verse Nephi explains why his people spoke of Christ so often.
ponder: Nephi names five ways his people kept Christ at the center. Which would you like to do more of?
Who might need to know “to what source they may look” for forgiveness?
What would it mean for you to ‘rejoice in Christ’ this week?
sessions.prayer: If you’d like, thank Heavenly Father for someone who has talked with you of Christ, and ask how you might do the same for someone else.

verses.text: And we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ, and we write according to our prophecies, that our children may know to what source they may look for a remission of their sins.
